# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and Definition

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP), increasingly termed "cardiac syndrome Y," is characterised by delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature during angiography in the absence of obstructive epicardial disease. It was first described in 1972 by Tambe and colleagues, who reported angina pectoris and slow flow velocity of dye in coronary arteries as a new angiographic finding [1]. Far from being a benign curiosity, coronary slow flow has clinical implications such as angina, acute coronary syndrome and sudden death [2]. Beltrame and colleagues subsequently reframed it as an angiographic finding characterized by delayed distal vessel opacification in the absence of significant epicardial coronary disease, proposing it as a distinct coronary microvascular disorder [3].

## Epidemiology and Clinical Presentation

CSFP is not rare. In a large angiographic series, CSFP was identified in 96 (5.5%) subjects referred for coronary angiography, and subjects with CSFP were more obese and had lower high-density lipoprotein levels [4]. Reported prevalence generally has an incidence of 1–5% in patients undergoing coronary angiography and has been most frequently found in young men who are smokers with metabolic syndrome [2]. The clinical burden is substantial: CSFP is a frequent finding in patients presenting with acute coronary syndromes, and over 80% of patients experience recurrent chest pain, resulting in considerable impairment in quality of life [5]. The presentation is heterogeneous, ranging from mild chest discomfort to ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction [6], and CSFP has been associated with ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death [7].

## Diagnosis

Diagnosis is angiographic. Historically, slow flow was identified subjectively, but this has been largely replaced by the corrected TIMI frame count (cTFC). The TIMI frame count was introduced by Gibson and colleagues as an objective, quantitative index of coronary blood flow as a continuous variable, counting the number of cineframes needed for dye to reach standardized distal landmarks [8]. Because the longer LAD frame counts were corrected by dividing by 1.7 to derive the corrected TIMI frame count [8]. In practice, diagnosis is made angiographically with either TIMI-2 flow or a corrected TIMI frame count of >27 frames, in addition to no angiographic lesions ≥40% [9]. Non-invasive alternatives are emerging: transthoracic Doppler echocardiography enables demonstration of coronary flow patterns in the LAD, with patients exhibiting lower coronary diastolic velocities that correlate negatively with cTFC [10].

Importantly, the relationship between angiographic slow flow and invasively measured microvascular dysfunction is debated. The COVADIS consensus statement included CSFP among diagnostic criteria for microvascular angina [11], yet recent invasive work suggests that angiographic coronary slow flow is not a valid surrogate for invasively diagnosed coronary microvascular dysfunction [12]. Conversely, other functional studies found that CSFP was associated with low flow velocity and higher microvascular resistance at rest compared with patients without CSFP [13].

## Pathophysiology

The mechanisms remain incompletely understood, but several converging themes exist. Histopathological studies of endomyocardial biopsies revealed small vessel thickening with luminal narrowing, dilated interstitial spaces, decreased intracellular glycogen, distorted mitochondrial cristae, and patchy myofibrillar disarray [14]. Earlier, Mosseri and colleagues provided histologic evidence for small-vessel coronary artery disease in patients with angina pectoris and patent large coronary arteries [15].

Endothelial dysfunction is a leading hypothesis. Camsari and colleagues demonstrated that endothelin-1 was higher and nitric oxide concentration was lower in patients with slow coronary flow than in matched controls, attributable to endothelial dysfunction [16]. Pekdemir and colleagues similarly linked plasma endothelin-1 and nitric oxide levels with heart rate variability in CSFP [17]. Sezgin and colleagues reported impaired vascular endothelial function in these patients [18]. CSFP has also been associated with diffuse subclinical atherosclerosis, as suggested by fractional flow reserve and intravascular ultrasound studies [19], and elevated homocysteine has been implicated [20]. However, not all data support endothelial dysfunction; Kopetz and colleagues found no differences between CSFP and controls in response to salbutamol or glyceryl trinitrate, and no differences in measured inflammatory and oxidative biomarkers [21]. Mechanistically, the most direct evidence comes from Beltrame and colleagues, who showed that resting coronary sinus oxygen saturation was low compared with control subjects, reflecting an increased basal coronary vasomotor tone [22]. Inflammation also appears relevant, with reports of increased C-reactive protein and interleukin-6 in affected patients [23].

## Clinical Consequences and Prognosis

CSFP can cause measurable electrophysiological and functional consequences. It is associated with increased QT dispersion [24], and prolonged P-wave duration with impaired diastolic filling [25]. In a large cohort study, 429 patients fulfilling criteria for CSFP were followed (mean 3.8 years), and major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 39 patients (9.3%) [26], indicating that the prognosis, while generally better than obstructive disease, is not entirely benign.

## Management

No definitive therapy exists, but several agents show promise. The strongest evidence is for calcium-channel blockade; Beltrame and colleagues found that the calcium T-channel blocker mibefradil reduced total angina frequency by 56% and sublingual nitroglycerine consumption by 59% over a 12-month period [27]. Intracoronary nifedipine acutely abolishes the angiographic finding [9]. Nebivolol improves endothelial function: in a study of CSFP patients, chest pain relief was detected in 90% after treatment, and high-sensitivity CRP was significantly decreased after nebivolol therapy [28]. Oral dipyridamole, which reduces microvascular tone, has also been reported as useful [29], and statins may improve myocardial perfusion through anti-inflammatory effects [30]. Overall, evidence for management is weak as there are no large randomised controlled trials, but calcium-channel blockers are the most promising treatment [2].

## Conclusion

CSFP is a clinically relevant entity affecting a meaningful proportion of patients undergoing angiography, frequently presenting with recurrent angina that impairs quality of life. Although microvascular and endothelial dysfunction, structural small-vessel changes, and inflammation are all implicated, the precise pathophysiology and its relationship to invasively-defined microvascular dysfunction remain contested. Diagnosis rests on the corrected TIMI frame count, and management is empirical, with calcium-channel blockers best supported. Larger randomised trials and standardised functional assessment are needed to clarify mechanisms and optimise therapy.
